transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello, Ms. Tremblay. I wanted to come in and talk with you about the reaction you had to the medication earlier today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The nurse already told me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. To be clear about what happened, you were given a dose of Ceftriaxone. That drug is a cephalosporin, and your chart explicitly lists an allergy to that class of antibiotics. The medication was ordered and administered despite that alert being in your record.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Does that make sense, or can I explain the drug interaction more clearly?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It makes sense. The system failed.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is incredibly frustrating to be in a position where you trust the staff with your care and then find out a basic piece of your medical history was ignored. I can imagine that feels like a real breach of trust, especially when you're just trying to get recovered and get back to your unit.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm more concerned about how long it takes to get the hives to go down. I have a flight in three days.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I completely hear that. Your priority is your timeline and getting back to duty. I know how important that window is for your deployment schedule.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Exactly. So how do we fix this?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We have you on a course of antihistamines and corticosteroids now to resolve the inflammation. I'll be monitoring your vitals every four hours. You'll need to let the nursing staff know immediately if you feel any tightness in your throat or if the itching worsens.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can do that.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll check your lungs again at 6:00 PM to make sure your breathing is totally clear. If the rash is gone by tomorrow morning, I'll sign off on the discharge papers so you can get home.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's what I need. Who actually signed the order?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The ordering process involves a few different screens. There was a gap in the verification process.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's not an answer. Did you sign it?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was processed through the residency team. The protocol for checking the allergy tab wasn't followed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is a pretty simple mistake to make.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know. It's a failure of the system. I'm going to have to get moving to the next room now, but I'll be back soon.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait, you're just leaving?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I just have to check on a few other patients quickly. We have the plan in place.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not saying I'm panicked, but I'm not exactly thrilled that I almost had a systemic reaction because someone didn't click a button.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see why you'd feel that way. It's a stressful situation and it's not how things should have gone. I'm really sensing how disappointing this is for you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It's not disappointing. It's incompetent.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand that perspective. It is a serious oversight.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Are you going to report this?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, an incident report has been filed. It goes to the quality review board to see how we can stop this from happening to other patients.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Fine.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll be back at 6:00. Just keep an eye on those hives and tell the nurse if they spread.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language ('I'm going to have to get moving to the next room now', 'I just have to check on a few other patients quickly') while the patient is expressing distress.

E.justification: Error named in the first turn, used lay language, checked comprehension ('Does that make sense?'), and provided a second check on breathing/rash.

A.justification: No direct apology language ('I'm sorry' or 'I apologize') is used, and responsibility is deflected to 'the system' and 'the ordering process'.

R.justification: Resident names specific emotions ('breach of trust', 'disappointing') and references the patient's specific concern regarding the deployment schedule.

T.justification: Plan includes specific steps (antihistamines, vitals every 4 hours, lung check at 6 PM), a patient role (notify staff of throat tightness), and prevention (incident report to quality review board).
